# Mathematical Visualization Reference Base

## Purpose

This file records transferable principles for mathematically driven visualization. It is not a license to copy source figures, applets, code, or distinctive layouts.

## 1. Primary reference class — visual and interactive mathematics

### Juan Carlos Ponce Campuzano — Complex Analysis: A Visual and Interactive Introduction

Public project:
- https://complex-analysis.com/
- https://github.com/jcponce
- https://github.com/jcponce/complex

User-provided Patreon reference:
- https://www.patreon.com/jcponce/posts/complex-analysis-115388302

The Patreon post itself was not directly retrievable during the 2026-10-06 repository update. The public Complex Analysis project and public GitHub profile/repositories were used for verifiable source grounding.

Source-supported characteristics of the public project:
- it presents complex analysis from a visual and interactive point of view;
- it uses interactive applets to explore mathematical properties geometrically;
- public repository metadata identifies p5.js, CindyJS, MathCell, and related visualization technologies across the project ecosystem;
- the project includes domain coloring, conformal mapping, Riemann surfaces, and other interactive mathematical views.

Transferable principle for this thesis:

\[
\boxed{
\text{mathematics drives the visual behavior}
}
\]

not:

\[
\text{equations placed inside decorative graphics}.
\]

### Permitted transfer

Use the reference to improve:
- model-to-visual mappings;
- parameter-driven interaction;
- time-driven animation;
- state-space visualization;
- threshold visualization;
- deterministic recomputation;
- transformation grammar;
- topology-preserving diagrams;
- visual comparison of trajectories and scenarios.

### Do not transfer

Do not copy:
- source-specific layouts;
- distinctive applet appearance;
- copyrighted illustrations;
- source code unless separately licensed and intentionally adopted;
- color schemes merely because they are visually attractive;
- domain coloring where the thesis variable does not mathematically justify it.

---

## 2. Scientific computing / dynamic visualization

Transferable lessons:
- separate model, solver, derived quantities, visual encoding, renderer, and interaction;
- prefer deterministic visual states;
- make temporal evolution traceable to simulation time;
- expose thresholds, feasible regions, and invariants when they are part of the model;
- recompute the mathematics before redrawing the visualization.

---

## 3. Systems engineering diagrams

Transferable lessons:
- boundary, environment, interface, state, service, control, and arrow semantics remain authoritative;
- mathematical visualization does not replace systems-engineering semantics;
- common hazard exposure must not be drawn as an interdependency;
- physical flow, demand/dependency, mathematical transformation, measurement, control, and feedback must remain graphically distinct.

---

## 4. Thesis-specific two-figure architecture

### Conceptual framework
No formulas.

Purpose:
- show the global scientific logic;
- show what affects what;
- show resilience and sustainability as distinct but connected outcomes;
- show SDG relevance/alignment only after sustainability consequences are identified.

### Mathematical framework
Formal equations.

Purpose:
- define state;
- define evolution;
- define transition time;
- define propagation timing;
- define service;
- define interventions;
- quantify resilience;
- quantify sustainability dimensions;
- define indicator-to-SDG-target interpretation.

The two figures must preserve the same scientific topology.

## Permanent project rule

\[
\boxed{
\text{Scientific visualization}
=
\text{formal scientific object}
+
\text{declared visual encoding}
+
\text{verified rendering}
}
\]

A visual effect without a mathematical or scientific mapping is decoration and should be removed.
